source.title: Ambiguous Fits: The Rashomon Effect and Challenges in Scaling Law Estimation

record.tranche_reason: The study's own fitting experiments show that near-optimal power-law fits can give substantially different extrapolations, and that initialization-grid choices affect fitted losses and prediction envelopes.
record.gate_note: The paper studies the fitting and extrapolation of power-law curves, not whether held-out language-model loss follows a power law across parameters, tokens, or compute, nor whether actual larger held-out runs match predictions. It mentions Delphi's large-scale runs as held-out evaluation data but reports no outcome comparing predictions with those runs. Results attributed to cited studies are not recorded.
record.test_reason: On four published LM validation-loss ladders (Apple DCLM, Delphi, Chinchilla/EpochAI, Llama 3), the study shows that the fitting procedure decides the fitted law and its extrapolation. The procedure is Chinchilla Approach 3: its initialization grid, and which of several near-equal fits it returns. This bears directly on V7's fitting-method part. It does not check predictions against real larger runs.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that heuristic Chinchilla-style fitting neither certifies near-optimality nor reveals that broad sets of near-equal fits extrapolate very differently. They propose certified branch-and-bound fitting and prediction envelopes. They add that envelope width is ultimately governed by earlier pipeline stages (ladder design, training, metric).
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes power-law fitting and extrapolation ambiguity using synthetic and previously published scaling ladders; it does not reproduce the original model-training experiments or test their scaling-law claims directly.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization-grid density and which optimization basins are reached affect fitting loss and the resulting prediction envelope; a denser non-nested grid can attain a worse fit.

fits_no_version.finding: On a synthetic ladder built to be ambiguous, two fits within about 1% of the certified optimum imply a 74.6× compute-efficiency gap at 300× the training range. The certified band at 3e23 FLOPs is [0.1202, 0.2392].
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Near-optimal power-law fits to a scaling ladder can be non-identifiable (a Rashomon effect), so a single fit understates extrapolation uncertainty.

record.problems: The four empirical ladders are previously published data, and some are digitized from figures. The empirical prediction envelopes in Figure 2 use local constrained searches and are stated to be inner approximations, not certified full envelopes. The study analyzes single-run observations and does not account for their randomness. It does not report outcomes for the mentioned held-out large-scale Delphi runs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results left out. Figure 2's dataset-specific envelope values are not reported numerically in the text, so they are not assigned separately; only the explicitly stated aggregate range is recorded in r3.

untested.parts: Parameter-counting conventions, training schedule, data changes, the compute-optimal N/D split, exponent disagreement across published laws, and curvature away from a single power law on real data.

Whether fitted laws match the actual loss of larger runs. The Delphi held-out runs up to 1e23 FLOPs are named but no comparison is reported. The prediction spread at 300× shows extrapolations are not uniquely determined, but it is not a measure of accuracy.
The power-law form is assumed, not tested.

missing.what: Certified suboptimality of Chinchilla Approach 3 at K=1..8 grid densities versus branch-and-bound, per ladder (fitting-method dependence of attained loss).
Anecdotal note that a log-residual objective gives lower extrapolation error than MSE or untransformed Huber (fitting-objective dependence). No numbers are given.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The Chinchilla ladder is EpochAI's re-digitization of Hoffmann et al. data, and the Llama 3 ladder is digitized from figures. Per-ladder envelope values are only shown graphically. The 14×–146× range comes from local-search inner approximations, so true envelopes can only be wider. Observations are single-seed runs and noise is not modelled. The V2 relevance is indirect: the study shows non-unique extrapolations, not wrong ones.

versions.untested_parts: The study assumes a power-law hypothesis class and does not test whether held-out pretraining loss follows a power law over several orders of magnitude.
It reports divergence among extrapolations from fits to small ladders, but does not report whether those fits predict observed losses of actual larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation trend or growth exponents are estimated.
The study does not compare architecture depth, width, or other architectural details at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer regime is tested.
Although one ladder includes downstream evaluations, the reported fitting and extrapolation results do not test downstream-task predictability.

Tests sensitivity to initialization grids and ambiguity among near-optimal fits. It does not test parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, changes to the training data, the compute-optimal split, or whether empirical curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Synthetic scaling ladder (Figure 1)
rows.operation_detail: Fit the standard three-parameter power law and compare predictions from near-optimal fits.
rows.measure: Compute-efficiency difference between viable fits for a target loss
rows.uncertainty: Certified prediction envelope; at 3 × 1023 FLOPs the loss band is [0.1202, 0.2392].
rows.locator: Figure 1; Appendix C, Figure 1 experimental details
rows.note: The synthetic ladder is generated from a continuous piecewise power law with multiplicative log-normal noise (σ = 0.02). The paper reports that two fits within 1% of the optimum imply the stated compute-efficiency difference.
rows.check: Synthetic ladder built from a piecewise power law chosen 'so that multiple near-optimal scaling laws can fit it well'. It is not LM loss and the ambiguity is induced on purpose, so it is an illustration, not a test of V7. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Synthetic scaling ladder (Figure 1)
rows.operation_detail: Compare fitting losses of two distinct L-BFGS fits to the same ladder.

conditions.value: Two fits initialized near the two piecewise components

rows.measure: Difference in fitting loss between fits
rows.value: The two fitting losses differ by less than 0.12%; the better fit is certified within 0.02% of the optimum, whose lower bound is 5.9198 × 10−5.
rows.uncertainty: Certified lower bound and optimality gap as stated.
rows.note: Near-equal fitting losses accompany materially different extrapolations; the extrapolation difference is recorded separately in r1.
rows.check: Same synthetic ladder as r1. It reports a fitting-loss certificate (0.12% difference, within 0.02% of optimum), which describes the method, not LM scaling behaviour. The 'baseline' is just the better fit's loss.

rows.subject: Four empirical scaling ladders (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Four ladders; individual run counts are stated in Appendix B.1
rows.operation_detail: Fit Chinchilla Approach 3 at the 55-initialization grid and search for fits with no worse fitting loss.

conditions.value: Apple DCLM, Delphi, Chinchilla (EpochAI), and Llama 3
300× the largest training compute, along D = 20 N

rows.measure: Range of compute-efficiency differences implied by fits in the reported sublevel sets
rows.value: Between 14× and 146× across the four ladders
rows.uncertainty: The extreme fits are found by local search; the paper says the true envelopes can only be wider.
rows.note: One aggregate row: the paper reports this range across the four datasets rather than giving these endpoints separately for each ladder.
rows.check: Value is right (14×–146× across ladders at the 5^5 grid). The comparison fits are those at least as good as the Chinchilla fit, which is itself 2–180% above the minimum, so the spread mixes optimization error with true ambiguity. Bands come from local search and are inner approximations.

source_check.correct: The 14×–146× compute-efficiency range compares extreme alternative fits at a common target loss. The returned Chinchilla fit supplies the fitting-loss threshold defining admissible alternatives; it is not the denominator of the reported compute-efficiency range.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3; Figure 2 caption; Appendix C, Figure 2 experimental details.
source_check.problem: The baseline conflates the fitting-loss reference with the compute-efficiency comparator.

rows.subject: Four empirical scaling ladders (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compare Chinchilla Approach 3 fits from different initialization-grid densities with the certified minimum.
rows.measure: Excess fitting loss over the minimum
rows.value: The 5^5 fits exceed the minimum by between 2% and 180% across the four ladders.
rows.uncertainty: Certified bounds on the minimum fitting loss.
rows.note: The result is reported as a range across ladders, not separately for each dataset.
rows.check: Correct: the 5^5 Chinchilla fits exceed the certified minimum by 2–180% across ladders. Separately, Section 4.4 says the Figure 2 Chinchilla fits are within 1e-5 of the optimum in absolute loss.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3, paragraph immediately before the discussion of near-optimal fits.

rows.subject: Four empirical scaling ladders (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Vary the initialization-grid density used for Chinchilla Approach 3 and compare resulting sublevel prediction envelopes.

conditions.value: K ∈ {2, 5, 8}, with K^5 initializations at each density

rows.measure: Change in prediction-envelope width as grid density increases
rows.value: Envelopes generally narrow as K increases.
rows.uncertainty: The paper notes that the grids are not nested and narrowing is not guaranteed.
rows.note: The statement is aggregate and qualified as a general tendency; numerical envelope widths are not given per density and dataset.
rows.check: The dependence of the envelope on grid density K is present; the narrowing is only 'generally' true and no numbers are given. State changed from partial, because the version's effect (dependence on a fitting choice) does appear.

rows.subject: Llama 3 IsoFLOP Suite
rows.operation_detail: Compare the best Chinchilla Approach 3 fit found from two non-nested initialization grids.
rows.value: The 2^5 grid attains a lower fitting loss than the 5^5 grid.
rows.note: The text explains that non-nested grids and which optimization basins are reached can make a denser grid perform worse.
rows.check: Correct; this is a qualitative statement with no numbers.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3, non-nested-grid example; Appendix B, Llama 3 dataset description.

relationships.condition: Four empirical LM ladders fitted with Chinchilla Approach 3 (5-parameter law, log-Huber loss, L-BFGS from K^5 grids)
relationships.reason: The grid choice changes the attained fit (r4, r6) and the envelope (r5). Fits at least as good as the returned one imply a 14×–146× compute-efficiency spread at 300× (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Initialization-grid choice changed the attained fit and prediction envelope, while equally good or better fits implied compute-efficiency spreads of 14×–146× at 300× extrapolation.

relation.reason: The study directly varies fitting choices on fixed empirical ladders and measures their effects on attained objectives and extrapolated predictions.

tranche.reason: The empirical refits and synthetic example show why single-fit scaling forecasts require qualification: heuristic optimization and nearly equivalent fits can yield substantially different extrapolations.

source_check.notes: Figure 2 envelopes are local-search inner approximations, not certified envelopes; their spread combines optimization error and fitting ambiguity. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; the study does not prospectively validate competing compute-optimal allocations.
